title: Networking & HTTP Fundamentals
pri: Never skip — everything sits on top of this

tops: OSI model — 7 layers and each layer's responsibility
TCP/IP model — 4 layers and mapping to OSI
IP addressing — IPv4, IPv6, CIDR, subnetting, NAT
TCP — 3-way handshake (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK)
TCP — 4-way teardown (FIN → FIN-ACK → FIN → ACK)
TCP flow control — sliding window protocol
TCP congestion control — slow start, AIMD, CUBIC
UDP — connectionless, no ordering, no guarantee, use cases
DNS resolution — recursive vs iterative, root → TLD → authoritative
DNS record types — A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, PTR, SOA
DNS TTL — caching behavior, propagation delay
Latency sources — propagation, transmission, queuing, processing
Bandwidth vs throughput — why they differ in practice
RTT (Round Trip Time) and its compounding effect on performance
HTTP/1.0 — new connection per request
HTTP/1.1 — persistent connections, pipelining, keep-alive, Head-of-Line blocking
HTTP/2 — multiplexing streams, header compression (HPACK), server push, binary framing
HTTP/3 — QUIC over UDP, 0-RTT connection, built-in TLS 1.3, no TCP HoL blocking
HTTPS — TLS handshake flow: ClientHello → ServerHello → Certificate → Key Exchange → Finished
TLS 1.2 vs TLS 1.3 — fewer round trips, no RSA key exchange (forward secrecy)
Mutual TLS (mTLS) — both client and server authenticate with certificates
Certificate chains — root CA → intermediate CA → leaf certificate
HTTP methods — GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS and idempotency of each
HTTP caching headers — Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified, If-None-Match, Vary
CORS — same-origin policy, preflight OPTIONS, Access-Control-Allow-* headers
Cookies — HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite (Strict/Lax/None), session vs persistent
Content negotiation — Accept, Content-Type, Accept-Encoding
REST — 6 constraints: stateless, uniform interface, cacheable, layered, client-server, code on demand
REST idempotency — GET/PUT/DELETE idempotent, POST not; why it matters for retries
GraphQL — schema, queries, mutations, subscriptions, N+1 problem, DataLoader batching solution
gRPC — Protocol Buffers, unary/server-streaming/client-streaming/bidirectional streaming
gRPC vs REST — binary vs text, schema contract, streaming, use cases for each
WebSockets — full-duplex, ws:// upgrade from HTTP, heartbeat ping-pong, reconnection
Server-Sent Events (SSE) — one-way server push over HTTP, auto-reconnect, use cases
Long polling — client holds connection until server has data, fallback for older clients
Webhooks — event-driven callbacks, retry policy, HMAC signature verification
API versioning strategies — URL path (/v1/), query param, header, content negotiation
Idempotency keys — safe retries for payments and mutations
WebRTC — peer-to-peer video/audio, STUN (IP discovery), TURN (relay), ICE negotiation
Forward proxy — client-side, hides client identity, corporate firewalls
Reverse proxy — server-side, hides server topology (Nginx, HAProxy)
API gateway — routing, auth enforcement, rate limiting, request aggregation, protocol translation
CDN — PoPs (Points of Presence), edge nodes, origin server, pull vs push model
CDN cache invalidation — TTL expiry, immediate purge, cache-busting via URL versioning
CDN for dynamic content — ESI (Edge Side Includes), Lambda@Edge, Cloudflare Workers
GeoDNS — route users to nearest datacenter based on client IP
Anycast routing — same IP announced from multiple locations, routed to nearest

note: Know the full request lifecycle cold: DNS lookup → TCP handshake → TLS handshake → HTTP request → server processing → HTTP response → browser render. Draw this on a whiteboard from memory.

title: Database Internals — SQL
pri: Every design involves a database decision

tops: Atomicity — all operations in a transaction succeed or all roll back
Consistency — DB moves from one valid state to another, constraints always satisfied
Isolation — concurrent transactions don't see each other's intermediate state
Durability — committed data survives crashes (WAL-based)
BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT — transaction control
Read Uncommitted — dirty reads allowed, fastest but rarely useful
Read Committed — no dirty reads, default in PostgreSQL and Oracle
Repeatable Read — same row read twice gives same result within transaction (MySQL default)
Serializable — strictest, prevents all anomalies including phantoms (SSI in PostgreSQL)
Dirty read — reading uncommitted data from a concurrent transaction
Non-repeatable read — same row returns different value on second read in same transaction
Phantom read — same range query returns different set of rows in same transaction
Lost update — two transactions read-modify-write the same row, one overwrites the other
Write skew — two transactions read overlapping data and make conflicting writes (e.g., on-call scheduling)
Shared lock (S) — multiple readers can hold simultaneously
Exclusive lock (X) — single writer holds, blocks all readers and writers
Intention locks (IS, IX, SIX) — hierarchical locking for efficiency
Two-Phase Locking (2PL) — growing phase (acquire only), shrinking phase (release only)
Strict 2PL — hold all exclusive locks until commit/abort (prevents cascading aborts)
Deadlock — circular wait: T1 holds A waits B, T2 holds B waits A
Deadlock detection — wait-for graph cycle detection
Deadlock prevention — lock ordering (always acquire in same order), timeout + retry
Deadlock resolution — abort the youngest transaction (wound-wait scheme)
MVCC — Multi-Version Concurrency Control: readers don't block writers, writers don't block readers
MVCC in PostgreSQL — each row has xmin/xmax visibility markers
Optimistic locking — read with version, update with WHERE version=N, check affected rows
Pessimistic locking — SELECT FOR UPDATE (acquires row-level lock)
SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — queue-like pattern for job workers
Predicate locks — Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) in PostgreSQL 9.1+
B+ tree index — leaf nodes contain data/row pointers linked in sorted order, O(log N) seek + range
Hash index — O(1) exact match, no range queries, used in Hash join, pg_trgm GIN
Composite index — column order matters: WHERE a=1 AND b=2 uses (a,b) but not (b,a) for a-only query
Covering index — index includes all queried columns, avoids table heap lookup (index-only scan)
Partial index — index on subset of rows with WHERE clause (e.g. WHERE status='active')
Expression / functional index — index on LOWER(email), EXTRACT(year FROM created_at)
Index selectivity — high cardinality = high selectivity = more useful index
Clustered index (InnoDB) vs heap storage (PostgreSQL) — physical row ordering differs
EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE — read execution plans: seq scan vs index scan vs bitmap
Query planner statistics — ANALYZE command, pg_statistic, histograms
N+1 query problem — fetch N parents then 1 query per parent; fix with JOIN or DataLoader batching
JOIN types — INNER, LEFT OUTER, RIGHT OUTER, FULL OUTER, CROSS, SELF JOIN
Window functions — ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG, LEAD, SUM/AVG OVER PARTITION
CTEs (Common Table Expressions) — WITH clause, readability, recursive CTEs for tree traversal
Lateral joins — correlated subquery in FROM clause, row-by-row evaluation
1NF — atomic values, no repeating groups
2NF — full functional dependency on entire primary key (no partial dependency)
3NF — no transitive dependency (non-key → non-key)
BCNF — every determinant is a candidate key
Denormalization — intentional redundancy to speed up reads, accept write overhead
Online schema changes — gh-ost (GitHub), pt-online-schema-change (Percona), pg_repack
Expand-contract pattern — add new column nullable → backfill → add constraint → drop old
Connection pooling — PgBouncer (transaction mode), HikariCP (JVM), Sequelize pool (Node)
PostgreSQL-specific — VACUUM, autovacuum, TOAST (for large values), pg_stat_activity
JSONB in PostgreSQL — binary JSON, GIN indexable, operators @>, ?, #>>
Full-text search in PostgreSQL — tsvector, tsquery, GIN index, ts_rank
Write-Ahead Log (WAL) — every change written to log before applied, enables crash recovery and replication
Checkpointing — periodically flush dirty pages to disk, bound WAL replay on restart

note: Know isolation levels cold. Classic interview trap: "two users book the last seat simultaneously — how do you prevent double booking?" → SELECT FOR UPDATE (pessimistic) vs optimistic locking + version check.

title: Database Scaling & NoSQL
pri: Every large-scale design depends on the right DB choice

tops: Read replicas — offload read traffic, replicate asynchronously from primary
Replication lag — async replica may be seconds behind; affects read-your-writes
Synchronous replication — write not confirmed until replica acks (low lag, higher latency)
Semi-synchronous replication — at least one replica must ack (MySQL)
Single-leader replication — all writes go to leader, replicated to followers
Multi-leader replication — writes to any datacenter, conflicts must be resolved
Leaderless replication — Dynamo style (Cassandra, Riak), any node accepts writes
Conflict resolution — last-write-wins (LWW), merge functions, custom CRDT
Replication factor — number of replicas (typically 3 for fault tolerance)
Read-your-writes consistency — user always sees their own writes, route writes and reads to same node
Monotonic reads — user never reads older data after reading newer data
Horizontal sharding — distribute rows of a table across multiple DB instances
Vertical partitioning — split different tables into different DBs by domain
Range-based sharding — shard by key range (user_id 1–1M on shard 1), easy range queries but hotspots
Hash-based sharding — hash(key) % N, even distribution, range queries hard
Consistent hashing for sharding — only K/N keys migrate when adding/removing nodes
Directory-based sharding — lookup service maps key to shard, flexible but single point of failure
Resharding — data migration challenge, double-write period, consistent hashing minimizes movement
Hot spots — celebrity rows, popular keys hitting same shard; solution: add random suffix
Cross-shard queries — scatter-gather (fan out to all shards), expensive, avoid in hot paths
Cross-shard transactions — two-phase commit risk, prefer Saga pattern instead
Shard key selection — high cardinality, even distribution, matches query pattern
MongoDB — documents, collections, BSON, replica sets, sharding (mongos + config servers)
MongoDB shard key selection — cardinality, write distribution, query isolation
MongoDB aggregation pipeline — $match, $group, $sort, $lookup, $project, $unwind
MongoDB transactions — multi-document ACID since v4.0 (distributed since v4.2)
Redis data structures — string, list, hash, set, sorted set, stream, HyperLogLog, bitmap, geo
Redis persistence — RDB (point-in-time snapshot) vs AOF (append-only log, fsync: always/everysec/no)
Redis Sentinel — HA: monitors master, auto-failover to replica on failure
Redis Cluster — shards data across 16384 hash slots, each node owns a range
Redis Streams — persistent ordered log with consumer groups (Kafka-lite)
Distributed lock with Redlock — acquire lock on N/2+1 nodes with short TTL, quorum-based safety
Cassandra data model — keyspace, table, partition key (distributes data), clustering key (orders within partition)
Cassandra write path — commit log → memtable → SSTable flush (LSM tree)
Cassandra read path — bloom filter check → SSTable cache → data files (from multiple SSTables)
Cassandra consistency levels — ONE, QUORUM, ALL, LOCAL_QUORUM, LOCAL_ONE
Cassandra gossip protocol — peer-to-peer O(log N) node state propagation
Cassandra hinted handoff — store writes for down nodes, replay when node recovers
Cassandra read repair — detect and fix stale replicas on read path
Cassandra anti-entropy — periodic Merkle tree comparison between replicas
Cassandra compaction — SizeTiered (write-heavy), Leveled (read-heavy), TWCS (time-series)
Cassandra tombstones — deleted data marked with timestamp, GC after gc_grace_seconds
DynamoDB — AWS managed, key-value + document, single-table design pattern
DynamoDB partition key + sort key, GSI (Global Secondary Index), LSI (Local)
DynamoDB hot partition — high-cardinality partition key is essential; write sharding for counters
Graph DB (Neo4j) — nodes, relationships, properties, Cypher query language
Time-series DB — InfluxDB, TimescaleDB (Postgres extension), Prometheus TSDB
Google Spanner — globally distributed, external consistency, TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks)
TrueTime — returns [earliest, latest] time interval, commit wait ensures monotonicity
CockroachDB — distributed Postgres-compatible, Raft consensus per range
TiDB — MySQL-compatible, separates compute (TiDB) from storage (TiKV with Raft)
YugabyteDB — PostgreSQL-compatible distributed SQL, uses DocDB storage engine
Aurora — MySQL/Postgres-compatible, shared distributed storage (6-way replication across 3 AZs)
Columnar storage — Parquet, ORC, Apache Arrow — for analytics, 10–100× faster than row stores
Column-oriented query execution — predicate pushdown, vectorized processing, compression
B-tree vs LSM-tree — B-tree: read-optimized (database indexes); LSM: write-optimized (Cassandra, RocksDB)
Write amplification in LSM trees — compaction rewrites data multiple times
Read amplification mitigated — bloom filter per SSTable level avoids unnecessary disk seeks

note: For every design: "Which database and why?" Practice the decision matrix: user profiles → PostgreSQL; social graph → Cassandra or Neo4j; session cache → Redis; time-series → InfluxDB/TimescaleDB; full-text search → Elasticsearch.

title: Caching — Every Layer
pri: Comes up in 80%+ of system design questions

tops: Cache-aside (lazy loading) — app checks cache, fetches DB on miss, populates cache
Read-through — cache layer fetches from DB on miss transparently to application
Write-through — write to cache and DB synchronously; reads always hit cache
Write-behind (write-back) — write to cache only, async flush to DB later; risk of data loss
Refresh-ahead — cache proactively refreshes keys before they expire based on access patterns
Negative caching — cache "not found" result with short TTL to prevent DB hammering on missing keys
Cache warming / pre-warming — populate cache before traffic spike (cold start problem)
Cache busting — append content hash to URLs to force new cache entries on deploy
LRU — Least Recently Used: evict the least recently accessed item (most common default)
LFU — Least Frequently Used: evict item with fewest accesses in time window
MRU — Most Recently Used: evict most recently accessed (good for sequential scans)
ARC — Adaptive Replacement Cache: dynamically balances LRU and LFU based on workload
TTL (Time To Live) — key expires after fixed duration, lazy deletion on access
Active expiry — background thread scans for expired keys (Redis probabilistic scan)
Redis maxmemory-policy — allkeys-lru, volatile-lru, allkeys-random, noeviction
Staggered TTLs — add small random jitter to TTL to prevent cache avalanche
Cache stampede / thundering herd — mass cache miss triggers simultaneous DB requests
Mutex lock to prevent stampede — only one request fetches, others wait and read populated cache
Probabilistic early re-expiration (PER) — randomly refresh before TTL expires to prevent stampede
Hot key problem — single key overwhelms one Redis node (e.g., celebrity tweet)
Hot key solution — local in-process L1 cache (Caffeine/Guava) + L2 Redis; key replication to N slots
Cache penetration — query for non-existent key repeatedly bypasses cache and hammers DB
Bloom filter for cache penetration — reject requests for keys known not to exist
Cache avalanche — mass TTL expiry at the same time causes thundering herd on DB
Staggered TTL + circuit breaker to handle cache avalanche
Cache consistency — dual write problem: cache + DB atomicity impossible without distributed transaction
Event-driven cache invalidation — use CDC (Debezium → Kafka) to invalidate on DB change
Client-side cache — browser cache, service worker, localStorage (for static assets)
In-process cache — Caffeine (JVM), Guava Cache, Node.js Map/LRU cache
Distributed cache — Redis, Memcached, Apache Ignite
Memcached vs Redis — Memcached: multi-threaded, pure cache; Redis: rich data types, persistence, Lua
Two-level cache architecture — L1 in-process (nanoseconds) + L2 Redis (microseconds)
CDN edge cache — CloudFront, Fastly, Cloudflare cache static and semi-static content
Reverse proxy cache — Nginx proxy_cache, Varnish Cache for HTTP response caching
Database query result cache — application-level, careful with invalidation
Redis Cluster for horizontal cache scaling — 16384 hash slots, add nodes to expand
Cache sizing estimation — working set size (hottest 20% of data), benchmark hit rate target >95%
Cache eviction monitoring — track eviction rate; high eviction means cache is too small

note: The thundering herd, cache stampede, and cache penetration are classic interview follow-up questions. Know the exact solutions for each: mutex lock / PER, bloom filter, staggered TTLs.

title: Scalability, Load Balancing & Infrastructure
pri: Applies to every system you will ever design

tops: Vertical scaling — bigger machine (more CPU, RAM, faster disk); simple but has hard limits and is expensive
Horizontal scaling — more machines; requires stateless design and coordination layer
Stateless services — no local state, any instance can serve any request; scale with load balancer
Stateful services — session affinity or external state store required
Distributed session — store sessions in Redis with TTL, enables stateless web servers
JWT for stateless auth — token carries identity, no server-side session store needed
Twelve-factor app — config in env, statelessness, logs as streams, disposability
Back-of-envelope estimation — QPS, storage, bandwidth, memory: always show arithmetic
QPS estimation — DAU × actions_per_day / 86400 seconds
Storage estimation — rows/day × row_size × retention_days × replication_factor
Bandwidth estimation — peak_QPS × average_response_size × peak_multiplier (×3–5)
Amdahl's Law — serial fraction limits maximum speedup: max = 1 / (S + (1-S)/N)
Little's Law — L = λW: avg items in system = arrival rate × avg time in system
Round robin — equal distribution ignoring server load or capacity
Weighted round robin — proportional to server CPU/memory/capacity
Least connections — route to server with fewest active connections (best for variable request duration)
IP hash — same client IP always routes to same server (sticky sessions without cookies)
Random with power of two choices — pick 2 random servers, route to least loaded (better than random)
Layer 4 LB — operates on TCP/UDP, fast, no HTTP awareness, no SSL termination
Layer 7 LB — operates on HTTP, content-aware routing, SSL termination, rewrites
DNS load balancing — multiple A records for same domain, TTL-based, no health checks
GSLB — Global Server Load Balancing, routes users to closest healthy datacenter
AWS ALB (L7) vs NLB (L4) vs Classic LB — ALB for HTTP/WebSocket, NLB for ultra-low latency TCP
Health checks — active (periodic HTTP probe) vs passive (monitor real traffic error rates)
Connection draining — grace period to complete in-flight requests before removing instance
Slow-start mode — gradually ramp up traffic to newly added instances to warm caches
Reactive auto-scaling — scale based on current CPU%, memory%, request count, queue depth
Predictive auto-scaling — pre-scale based on historical patterns (Black Friday, match kicks off)
AWS Auto Scaling Groups — min/desired/max, scale-out fast, scale-in slow (cooldown)
Kubernetes HPA — Horizontal Pod Autoscaler based on CPU/memory or custom metrics
Kubernetes VPA — Vertical Pod Autoscaler: right-sizes CPU/memory requests automatically
KEDA — Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling: scale on Kafka lag, SQS queue depth, etc.
Spot / preemptible instances — 70–90% cheaper with 2-min interruption notice; use for stateless batch
Serverless auto-scaling — Lambda scales to thousands of concurrent executions automatically
Scale-to-zero — Lambda, Cloud Run: no instances running when no traffic (cold start tradeoff)
Docker — image layers, Dockerfile best practices (multi-stage build, minimal base image)
Container vs VM — process isolation vs full OS, millisecond vs second startup time
Kubernetes control plane — API server (gateway), scheduler (pod placement), controller manager, etcd (cluster state)
Kubernetes worker nodes — kubelet (runs pods), kube-proxy (network rules), container runtime (containerd)
Pod, Deployment, Service (ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer), Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret, PVC
Rolling update — replace pods gradually; rollback on failure
StatefulSet — stable network identity, ordered deployment (Kafka, Cassandra, databases)
DaemonSet — one pod per node (log collectors, node-level monitoring, Istio sidecar)
Kubernetes resource requests vs limits — request = scheduling guarantee, limit = throttle ceiling
Node affinity, taints and tolerations — control which pods run on which nodes
Service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) — sidecar Envoy proxy, mTLS between services, traffic management, observability
Helm — Kubernetes package manager, templated manifests, release management

note: Always show your back-of-envelope math before jumping to architecture. "Given 10M DAU with 5 actions per day, that's ~578 QPS average, so design for 3K QPS peak." This shows engineering maturity.

title: Distributed Systems Fundamentals
pri: This is where SDE-2 interviews are WON or LOST

tops: CAP theorem — Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance: only 2 guaranteed when partition occurs
CP systems — prioritize consistency over availability during partition (ZooKeeper, HBase, etcd)
AP systems — prioritize availability over consistency during partition (Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB)
PACELC — when no Partition: tradeoff between Latency and Consistency (extends CAP)
BASE — Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent (NoSQL philosophy)
Linearizability — strongest: operation appears atomic at a single point in time, most recent write always visible
Sequential consistency — operations appear in program order but no global real-time guarantee
Causal consistency — causally related operations ordered, concurrent operations may differ
Read-your-writes — you always see your own writes (weaker than linearizability)
Monotonic reads — reads never go backwards in time (you never see older data after seeing newer)
Eventual consistency — given no new writes, all replicas converge to same value eventually
Strong eventual consistency — concurrent updates resolve deterministically without coordination (CRDTs)
Raft — leader election (randomized timeout, first to get majority votes), log replication, safety
Raft leader election — each node has random election timeout; first to expire sends RequestVote
Raft log replication — leader appends entry, replicates to majority, only then commits
Raft safety property — at most one leader per term, committed entries are never lost
Paxos — prepare/promise phase → accept/accepted phase (conceptual, harder to implement than Raft)
Multi-Paxos — designate stable leader to avoid repeated prepare phase
Zookeeper Atomic Broadcast (ZAB) — Zookeeper's proprietary consensus protocol
etcd — Raft-based distributed KV store, used by Kubernetes for all cluster state
Zookeeper — Apache, used for leader election (ephemeral znodes), distributed locks, config
Leader election with Zookeeper — create sequential ephemeral znode, watch predecessor
Epoch numbers / terms — monotonically increasing, stale leaders reject writes with old epoch
Fencing tokens — monotonically increasing token for storage writes, prevents stale leader writes
Split-brain — two nodes both think they are leader; prevent with fencing tokens + quorum
Physical clocks — NTP synchronization, drift up to 100ms between nodes
Clock skew — two machines have different wall clock times, cannot use for ordering events
Lamport timestamps — logical clocks: increment on send, max(local,received)+1 on receive, establish happens-before
Vector clocks — per-node counters: detect causality and concurrency, identify conflicting writes
Version vectors — detect divergence during replica synchronization
Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) — combine physical + logical: max(physical, last_hlc) + 1
Google TrueTime — GPS + atomic clocks, returns [earliest, latest] uncertainty interval (~7ms)
Commit wait (Spanner) — wait out TrueTime uncertainty before returning commit timestamp
Happens-before (→) — a→b means a causally precedes b; defines partial order of events
Total order vs partial order — total: every pair comparable; partial: concurrent events possible
Monotonic clock — use for measuring elapsed time; wall clock for human-readable timestamps
Quorum reads/writes — N replicas, write to W, read from R; W+R>N ensures overlap and consistency
Common quorum config — N=3, W=2, R=2: tolerates 1 failure, consistent reads
Gossip protocol — epidemic broadcast: each node periodically exchanges state with random peers, O(log N) convergence
Phi accrual failure detector — adaptive: outputs suspicion value φ, not binary up/down judgment
Read repair — detect stale replica during read, return latest to client, async update stale replica
Anti-entropy repair — Merkle tree comparison between nodes, repair differences in background
Hinted handoff — store writes for unavailable nodes locally, replay when node recovers
CRDTs — Conflict-free Replicated Data Types: G-counter, PN-counter, LWW-Register, OR-Set, 2P-Set
At-most-once delivery — fire and forget, may lose messages (UDP, basic HTTP without retry)
At-least-once delivery — retry until ack; messages may be duplicated, require idempotent consumers
Exactly-once semantics — hardest: Kafka transactions + idempotent producer + consumer isolation
Idempotency key pattern — include unique key in request; server deduplicates and returns same result
Distributed locks — Redis Redlock (quorum on N instances), Zookeeper ephemeral node, etcd lease
Distributed transactions — 2PC (coordinator blocks on failure), Saga (compensating transactions)
Two-phase commit — Phase 1: prepare (all vote), Phase 2: commit (if all yes) / abort (if any no)
Two-phase commit blocking problem — if coordinator crashes after prepare, cohorts wait forever
Saga pattern — sequence of local transactions with compensating transactions on failure
Saga choreography — services react to events published by previous service (loose coupling)
Saga orchestration — central saga orchestrator explicitly calls each service (easier to monitor)
Exponential backoff + jitter — prevent retry storms: wait = min(cap, base × 2^attempt) + rand(0, base)

note: Read DDIA (Kleppmann) Chapters 5–9 cover-to-cover before your interview. This phase is the biggest differentiator. Know Raft consensus, vector clocks, quorum NWR formula, and Saga pattern in depth.

title: Messaging & Event-Driven Architecture

tops: Point-to-point queue — one message consumed by exactly one consumer (work queue pattern)
Publish-subscribe topic — one message delivered to all subscribed consumers
Pull consumer model — consumer polls for messages (Kafka, SQS); consumer controls pace
Push consumer model — broker pushes to consumer (RabbitMQ); simpler but broker must manage rate
Message durability — persisted to disk (Kafka, SQS) vs in-memory (RabbitMQ default)
Message ordering — FIFO within partition (Kafka), not across partitions; SQS FIFO queues for order
Dead letter queue (DLQ) — messages that fail after N retries go here for inspection
Poison pill message — causes consumer to crash; detect with retry count, send to DLQ
Message deduplication — use idempotency key; consumer maintains processed-IDs set (inbox table)
Backpressure — slow consumer signals producer to slow down; Kafka: consumer controls offset commit rate
Fan-out pattern — one event triggers multiple independent consumers (order placed → payment + inventory + email)
Competing consumers — multiple workers on same queue share load, each message processed once
Message schema evolution — Avro/Protobuf compatibility modes: backward (reader handles old schema), forward (reader handles new schema), full
Topic — named logical stream of records
Partition — unit of parallelism; messages ordered within partition, not across
Offset — position of message within partition; unique and monotonically increasing
Consumer group — each partition consumed by exactly one consumer in group; parallelism = partition count
Producer acks — acks=0 (fire and forget), acks=1 (leader only), acks=all (all ISR must ack)
ISR (In-Sync Replicas) — set of replicas fully caught up to leader; min.insync.replicas threshold
Exactly-once semantics — enable.idempotence=true + transactional.id + consumer isolation=read_committed
Consumer lag — latest_offset - committed_offset per partition; monitor to detect slow consumers
Compacted topics — retain only latest value per key; used for changelogs, Kafka as database
Kafka Streams — stream processing library: stateful transformations with RocksDB local state stores
Kafka Connect — source connectors (DB → Kafka) and sink connectors (Kafka → DB/S3)
Schema Registry — Avro/Protobuf schema storage, compatibility enforcement on produce/consume
Kafka transactions — atomic multi-partition produce + offset commit
Retention — by time (retention.ms) or size (retention.bytes), not by consumer acknowledgement
Log compaction — background thread merges segments, keeps latest value per key
RabbitMQ — exchanges (direct, fanout, topic, headers), bindings, routing keys, queues
RabbitMQ vs Kafka — traditional message broker vs distributed log; RabbitMQ: complex routing; Kafka: replay, high throughput
AWS SQS Standard — at-least-once, best-effort ordering, up to 1 MiB, infinite scale
AWS SQS FIFO — exactly-once processing, ordered within message group, 300 TPS (3000 with batching)
AWS SNS — pub/sub fan-out to SQS, Lambda, HTTP, email, SMS; no replay
AWS Kinesis Data Streams — real-time, 1MB/s per shard, 7-day retention, replay capable
Google Cloud Pub/Sub — managed pub/sub, at-least-once, ordering per ordering-key, push or pull
Apache Pulsar — tiered storage (offload to S3), geo-replication, multi-tenancy, unified queue+stream
NATS — ultra-lightweight, sub-millisecond latency, JetStream for persistence
Event sourcing — append-only log of domain events is source of truth; current state = replay of events
Event store — immutable, ordered, replayable; projections rebuild read models
CQRS — Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate write model (commands) from read model (queries)
CQRS read models — optimized for query patterns, updated asynchronously via events
Outbox pattern — write event to outbox table in same DB transaction as domain change; relay process publishes to MQ
Inbox pattern — idempotent consumer with inbox table to deduplicate duplicate deliveries
Change Data Capture (CDC) — Debezium reads DB write-ahead log → publishes to Kafka; zero-impact on DB
Saga choreography vs orchestration — choreography: loose coupling, hard to trace; orchestration: central control, easier to monitor
Event versioning and upcasting — handle schema changes by transforming old events to new schema on read
Temporal coupling problem — synchronous chains; fix with async events to decouple services

note: The Outbox pattern is essential for atomic database write + message publish. Without it, you risk publishing an event for a transaction that later rolled back, or missing events for committed transactions.

title: Microservices & Architecture Patterns
pri: Core for SDE-2 role design discussions

tops: Monolith — single deployable unit; simple to start, becomes bottleneck as team grows
Modular monolith — well-structured monolith with clear module boundaries; intermediate step
Microservices — small, independently deployable services; each owns its data and API
Microservices trade-offs — independent scaling, independent deploy, team autonomy vs network latency, distributed transactions, operational complexity
Domain-Driven Design (DDD) — model software around business domain
Bounded context — explicit boundary within which a domain model applies (defines service boundary)
Aggregate root — consistency boundary: all changes go through root entity
Domain events — things that happened in the domain; trigger side effects in other bounded contexts
Ubiquitous language — shared vocabulary between engineers and domain experts within bounded context
Strangler fig pattern — incrementally migrate monolith: route traffic to new service, deprecate old endpoint
Anti-corruption layer — translation layer between old and new domain models
Shared kernel — small, carefully managed shared domain model between two contexts
Database per service — each service owns its DB; prevents tight coupling through shared schema
Shared database antipattern — multiple services sharing one DB creates deployment and schema coupling
Synchronous (REST, gRPC) — immediate response; temporal coupling: caller blocks, dependency failures cascade
Asynchronous (events, queues) — decoupled in time; harder to trace, but more resilient
Service discovery — how services find each other's network location dynamically
Client-side discovery — service queries registry (Eureka), load balances itself
Server-side discovery — load balancer queries registry (AWS ALB + ECS, Kubernetes Service)
Service registry — Consul (with health checks), Eureka, Kubernetes DNS (CoreDNS)
Circuit breaker pattern — closed (normal) → open (fail fast after threshold) → half-open (test recovery)
Hystrix (deprecated) / Resilience4j (Java) / Polly (.NET) — circuit breaker implementations
Retry with exponential backoff + jitter — avoid thundering herd on retry storms
Timeout — always set explicit timeouts; cascading timeouts cause full-stack slowdowns
Bulkhead pattern — separate thread pools/connection pools per dependency; one slow dep can't exhaust all threads
Fallback — return cached/default response when dependency fails (graceful degradation)
Idempotent APIs — safe to retry; critical for distributed systems where retries are unavoidable
Sidecar pattern — inject cross-cutting concerns (proxy, logging, mTLS) as sidecar container
Ambassador pattern — outbound proxy that adds retry/timeout/circuit-breaker to legacy services
Health endpoints — /health (is process running?), /ready (can accept traffic?), /live (Kubernetes liveness)
API gateway — single entry point: routing, auth enforcement, rate limiting, SSL termination, request aggregation
Backend for Frontend (BFF) — separate API layer per client type (iOS, Android, web, third-party)
API composition — gateway aggregates multiple downstream service calls into one response
Pagination — offset-based (simple, inconsistent with concurrent mutations) vs cursor-based (consistent, scales)
Filtering, sorting, field selection (sparse fieldsets) in REST API design
GraphQL federation — compose multiple subgraph schemas into unified API (Apollo Federation)
Rate limiting at gateway — token bucket per API key/user, per endpoint; return 429 with Retry-After header
OAuth 2.0 authorization code + PKCE — for SPA and mobile (prevents authorization code interception)
OAuth 2.0 client credentials — for server-to-server, no user involved
OpenID Connect (OIDC) — authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0: ID token (JWT) carries user identity
JWT structure — header (alg, typ) + payload (sub, iss, aud, exp, iat) + signature (HMAC-SHA256 or RS256)
JWT validation — verify signature, check exp, iss, aud claims; short expiry + refresh token rotation
API contract testing — Pact (consumer-driven contracts): consumer defines expectations, provider verifies
OpenAPI / Swagger specification — machine-readable API contract, enables code generation
Blue-green deployment — two identical environments; instant cutover by switching load balancer target
Canary release — route 1–5% of traffic to new version, monitor error rate, gradually increase
Feature flags — decouple code deploy from feature release; enable per user/segment
A/B testing — route users to variants statistically, measure conversion/engagement
Rolling deployment — incrementally replace pods/instances with new version (Kubernetes default)
Immutable infrastructure — never patch running instances; replace with new image from scratch
GitOps — Git as source of truth for desired state; ArgoCD/Flux reconciles cluster to match
CI/CD pipeline — source → build → unit test → integration test → security scan → artifact → staging → production
Expand-contract (parallel change) — add new field, backfill, then remove old field across two deploys
Database migration strategy in zero-downtime deploy — never use ALTER that locks table on production

note: Know circuit breaker states (closed/open/half-open) and the difference between choreography (events, loose coupling) vs orchestration (saga orchestrator, easier to trace). Both come up in every microservices discussion.

title: Cloud, Security & DevOps
pri: Expected at SDE-2 — shows production maturity

tops: EC2 — VMs, instance types (compute/memory/storage-optimized), placement groups, AMI
Lambda — serverless functions, event-driven, 15-min max, 10GB max memory, pay per GB-second
ECS — Docker container orchestration, Fargate (serverless) vs EC2 launch type
EKS — managed Kubernetes, control plane managed by AWS
S3 — object storage: bucket + key model, 50TB max object, strong consistency since 2021
S3 features — versioning, lifecycle policies, presigned URLs (time-limited access), multipart upload, replication, S3 Select
EBS — block storage attached to EC2, like a hard drive; one AZ, snapshot to S3
EFS — managed NFS, shared file system across multiple EC2 instances in same region
RDS — managed relational DB: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server; Multi-AZ for HA
Aurora — MySQL/Postgres-compatible, 6-way storage replication across 3 AZs, auto-scaling storage
DynamoDB — fully managed NoSQL, single-digit ms latency, automatic sharding
ElastiCache — managed Redis or Memcached in VPC
SQS / SNS / Kinesis / MSK — managed messaging; MSK = managed Kafka
VPC — isolated virtual network; public subnets (internet-facing), private subnets (internal)
Security Groups — stateful firewall at instance level; NACLs — stateless at subnet level
Route53 — DNS with health checks, routing policies: simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation
CloudFront — CDN, Lambda@Edge for edge compute, TLS termination, WAF integration
IAM — identity and access management: users, groups, roles, policies, least privilege
KMS — key management service: envelope encryption, key rotation, CloudTrail audit
CloudWatch — metrics, logs, alarms, dashboards; X-Ray for distributed tracing
Lambda cold starts — JVM/Python faster than Java; reduce with provisioned concurrency, SnapStart
Lambda concurrency — reserved concurrency (cap), provisioned concurrency (pre-warmed)
Lambda + SQS — reserved concurrency = backpressure; SQS retains messages, Lambda scales
Step Functions — stateful serverless workflows: sequential, parallel, wait, retry, catch
EventBridge — serverless event bus: route events from AWS services and SaaS to Lambda/SQS
Terraform — declarative IaC: resources, providers, state file (lock with S3 + DynamoDB)
Terraform plan/apply workflow — preview changes before applying; destroy with care
CloudFormation — AWS-native IaC: stacks, change sets, drift detection
Ansible — configuration management: agentless, idempotent YAML playbooks
Container registry — ECR (AWS), Docker Hub, GCR, Harbor (self-hosted)
GitOps with ArgoCD — desired state in Git, ArgoCD reconciles cluster continuously
CI/CD stages — build → unit test → integration test → security scan → artifact publish → deploy to staging → smoke test → promote to production
Authentication vs authorization — who are you (authn) vs what can you do (authz)
OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow + PKCE — for SPA/mobile: code_verifier + code_challenge prevent interception
OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow — service-to-service, no user context
JWT validation — verify signature (RS256 public key), check exp, iss, aud; never skip validation
Refresh token rotation — issue new refresh token on every use; revoke old one (prevents token theft)
Token storage — httpOnly+Secure cookies (XSS-resistant) vs localStorage (XSS risk)
API keys — rotate regularly, hash before storage (like passwords), scope by service
mTLS — both client and server present X.509 certificates; used for service-to-service auth in production
Encryption at rest — AES-256, transparent encryption (TDE), or field-level encryption
Encryption in transit — TLS 1.2/1.3 everywhere; enforce in security groups / policies
Secret management — HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager; never hardcode secrets
OWASP Top 10 — SQL injection, XSS, SSRF, broken access control, insecure deserialization — know each
SSRF — Server-Side Request Forgery: prevent by validating/blocking internal IP ranges in outbound requests
SQL injection — always parameterized queries, never string concatenation for SQL
DDoS mitigation — rate limiting (WAF), CDN absorption, IP reputation lists, Anycast
Zero-trust architecture — never trust, always verify; microsegmentation, device health checks
Principle of least privilege — every service/user gets minimum permissions needed
Audit logging — immutable log: who accessed what, when, from where; ship to SIEM
GDPR / PII handling — data minimization, right to erasure, encryption, data subject rights
Data masking and tokenization — protect PII in non-production environments

note: Even if not a DevOps engineer, SDE-2 interviews at product companies expect you to know how your service deploys, how it's monitored, and how it handles auth. Know IAM roles, JWT validation, and CI/CD pipeline stages.

title: Advanced Data Structures Used in Systems
pri: Shows depth — interviewers reward knowing the "why"

tops: Bloom filter — space-efficient probabilistic set: no false negatives, tunable false positive rate
Bloom filter FP rate — (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k where k=hash functions, n=items, m=bits
Bloom filter use cases — Cassandra SSTable key lookup, Redis key existence, DB query cache penetration
Counting Bloom filter — allows deletions by using counters instead of bits
Cuckoo filter — more space-efficient than Bloom for same FP rate, supports deletions, better cache locality
HyperLogLog — cardinality estimation: count distinct values with ~1.5% error using O(m) space
HyperLogLog in Redis — PFADD (add), PFCOUNT (estimate), PFMERGE (combine); used for daily active users
Count-Min Sketch — frequency estimation in data streams: O(ε,δ) space, approximate top-K
MinHash — estimate Jaccard similarity between sets; used for near-duplicate detection
Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) — hash similar items to same bucket; approximate nearest neighbor
Consistent hashing — arrange nodes on ring; key maps to next clockwise node; only K/N keys remap on node change
Virtual nodes (vnodes) — each physical node owns N virtual positions on ring; better load balance
Consistent hashing math — with V vnodes per node, variance of load = O(1/V); common: V=150
Rendezvous hashing (HRW) — score = hash(key + node), assign to highest score; O(1) per lookup
Jump consistent hash — O(1) space, deterministic, minimal disruption; used in Guava
Geohash — encode (lat, lng) to base32 string; proximity = shared prefix; grid cells of varying size
Geohash edge cases — cells near the poles, cells on the prime meridian; requires neighbor search
Quadtree — recursively subdivide 2D space into 4 quadrants; density-adaptive; used in Uber, Twitter
R-tree — spatial index for rectangles and polygons; used in PostGIS, MySQL Spatial, SQLite R*Tree
Google S2 — spherical geometry using Hilbert curve; uniform cell sizes at each level; used by Uber, Foursquare
Uber H3 — hexagonal hierarchical grid; constant area per cell; better for analytics than quadtree
B+ tree — all data in leaf nodes linked in sorted order; O(log N) search + efficient range scans; used in all RDBMS
LSM tree — MemTable → immutable SSTable → leveled compaction; write-optimized; used in Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB
LSM read path — check bloom filter (each level) → check SSTable index → read data block; amortized O(log^2 N)
Skip list — probabilistic balanced structure; O(log N) average search/insert; used in Redis sorted sets
Trie (prefix tree) — O(m) lookup by prefix where m = key length; used in autocomplete, IP routing
Compressed trie (Patricia/Radix tree) — merge single-child nodes; O(m) space instead of O(m²)
Inverted index — term → postings list (docID, frequency, position offsets); foundation of all search engines
Term dictionary — sorted list of all terms; binary search or trie for lookup; stored in SSTable-like format
Merkle tree — hash tree: leaf = hash(data), parent = hash(children); detect inconsistencies between replicas
Merkle tree in Cassandra — compare replicas without transferring all data; send tree hashes instead
Segment tree — range query (sum, min, max) in O(log N) with O(N) space; used in real-time analytics
Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) — range sum in O(log N) with simpler implementation than segment tree
UUID v4 — 128-bit random; globally unique with 2^122 possibilities; not sortable, no ordering
UUID v7 (new standard) — 48-bit Unix timestamp ms + 74-bit random; sortable, monotone within ms
ULID — 48-bit timestamp + 80-bit random; lexicographically sortable; URL-safe base32 encoding
Twitter Snowflake ID — 64-bit: 1 sign bit + 41 timestamp (ms, 69yr range) + 10 machine ID + 12 sequence (4096 IDs/ms)
Snowflake clock skew problem — if system clock goes back, ID generation pauses or errors
Instagram shard ID — 41-bit epoch ms + 13-bit shard ID + 10-bit sequence; generated in PostgreSQL
NanoID — URL-safe alphabet, configurable length, cryptographically random, similar collision prob to UUID
Ticket server (Flickr-style) — centralized DB auto-increment; simple but single point of failure
Monotonic IDs — crucial for sort order in databases and for Kafka partition ordering; avoid UUID as PK

note: Bloom filter and consistent hashing come up in almost every large-scale design. Know the false positive rate formula for Bloom filters. Know why virtual nodes solve the uneven distribution problem in consistent hashing.

title: Search, Analytics & Real-Time Systems
pri: Frequently asked at product companies (Google, Meta, LinkedIn)

tops: Web crawler — BFS URL frontier with priority queue; politeness: per-domain rate limit, robots.txt, crawl-delay
URL deduplication — canonical URL normalization + Bloom filter to avoid recrawling
Inverted index construction — tokenize → normalize → build term→postings list mapping
Postings list — docID + term frequency + position offsets; sorted by docID for merge operations
TF-IDF — term frequency (how often term appears in doc) × inverse document frequency (log(N/df))
BM25 — improved TF-IDF: saturates term frequency, normalizes by document length; default in Elasticsearch
Tokenization — split text on whitespace and punctuation; language-specific tokenizers (ICU, MeCab for Japanese)
Stemming — reduce words to root form (running → run); Porter, Snowball stemmers
Lemmatization — context-aware stemming (better → good); computationally heavier than stemming
Stop words — filter high-frequency words (the, a, is) to reduce index size
Elasticsearch cluster — master node (cluster state), data nodes (store/query shards), coordinating nodes
Elasticsearch shard — Lucene index; primary + replica; max ~50GB per shard for performance
Elasticsearch queries — match (full-text), term (exact), bool (must/should/must_not/filter), range, fuzzy, phrase, nested
Elasticsearch aggregations — terms (counts), date_histogram, stats, percentiles, nested agg
Autocomplete — edge n-gram analyzer (index), completion suggester (FST-based, very fast)
Spell correction — edit distance (Levenshtein), phonetic matching (Soundex, Metaphone)
Faceted search — aggregations + post_filter; show category/price/brand counts alongside results
Search relevance tuning — field boosting (title^3), function_score (recency), learning to rank
Index lifecycle management (ILM) — hot → warm → cold → delete phases for time-series indices
Dense vector embeddings — neural encoder maps text/image to fixed-dim float vector in semantic space
Semantic search — find similar meaning, not exact keyword match; handles synonyms, paraphrases
Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) — find K most similar vectors without exhaustive search
HNSW — Hierarchical Navigable Small World: graph-based ANN, O(log N) query, best recall/speed tradeoff
FAISS — Meta's ANN library: IVF (inverted file index) + PQ (product quantization for compression)
Vector databases — Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, Qdrant, pgvector (Postgres extension)
Hybrid search — BM25 keyword + dense vector; combine with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
Embedding models — text-embedding-3-small (OpenAI), BERT, BGE, E5, Cohere Embed
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) — vector search retrieves context, LLM generates answer
Re-ranking — cross-encoder (slower, higher quality) re-ranks top-K ANN results for final list
OLTP vs OLAP — row-oriented (many small writes) vs columnar (analytical aggregations)
Star schema — fact table (events) + dimension tables (who, what, when, where); Kimball model
Snowflake schema — normalized dimensions; reduces redundancy but more JOINs
Columnar storage — Parquet, ORC: compress and encode columns together; 10–100× faster for analytics
Data warehouse — Snowflake (cloud-native), BigQuery (serverless), Redshift (columnar, AWS)
Data lake — raw files in S3/GCS, queried via Athena/Presto on-demand; flexible but no ACID
Lakehouse — ACID transactions on data lake; Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi
Batch processing — Apache Spark: RDD, DataFrame, Spark SQL, lazy evaluation, Catalyst optimizer
Stream processing — Apache Flink: event time vs processing time, watermarks, stateful operators, exactly-once
Kafka Streams — lightweight stream processing: stateful with embedded RocksDB, runs inside application
Lambda architecture — batch layer (Spark, correctness) + speed layer (Flink, low latency) + serving layer
Kappa architecture — stream-only using Kafka as event log; reprocess historical data by replaying from offset 0
ELT vs ETL — load raw first then transform (ELT with dbt) vs transform before loading (ETL with SSIS/Informatica)
Apache Airflow — workflow orchestration: DAGs, schedulers, workers, metadata DB; define pipelines as code
CDC with Debezium — reads DB WAL (binary log) → publishes change events to Kafka; zero impact on source DB
ClickHouse — columnar OLAP engine, 100–1000× faster than MySQL for aggregations, real-time ingestion
Apache Druid — real-time OLAP: ingest from Kafka, sub-second queries, time-series optimized
Presto / Trino — federated SQL query engine: query S3, Hive, Cassandra, MySQL with single SQL
WebSocket upgrade — HTTP Upgrade header (101 Switching Protocols), then full-duplex ws:// protocol
WebSocket scalability — fan-out via Redis Pub/Sub across multiple WebSocket server instances
Server-Sent Events — HTTP streaming, server pushes events, client auto-reconnects; simpler than WebSocket
Long polling — client holds connection (30s timeout) until event; reconnects immediately after response
Real-time presence system — heartbeat every 30s with TTL=60s in Redis; expire = offline; publish change via Pub/Sub
Live leaderboard — Redis sorted set: ZADD adds score, ZRANGE gets rank, ZRANK gets position; push via WebSocket
Real-time collaborative editing — OT (Operational Transformation, Google Docs) vs CRDT (conflict-free, Figma, Notion)
Online gaming — authoritative server model, UDP for state updates, client-side prediction + reconciliation
Real-time location tracking — GPS → WebSocket → geospatial index (Redis GEO or Quadtree) → nearby query
Live streaming — RTMP ingest → transcode (FFmpeg) → HLS segmentation → CDN origin → edge → viewer
Adaptive bitrate streaming — HLS/DASH: multiple quality levels; client switches based on bandwidth
Real-time counters at scale — Redis INCR + async batch flush to DB every N seconds; eventual consistency

note: For search design: always cover the crawl → build inverted index → serve pipeline. For real-time: explain exactly how a message from User A reaches User B's browser — WebSocket → backend → Redis Pub/Sub → user's server → WebSocket → browser.

title: Reliability, Observability, Performance & Security
pri: Expected at SDE-2 — production maturity signal

tops: SLA — Service Level Agreement: contractual uptime commitment (e.g., 99.9% uptime per month)
SLO — Service Level Objective: internal target (e.g., p99 latency < 200ms, error rate < 0.1%)
SLI — Service Level Indicator: the actual measured metric (e.g., % of requests completing < 200ms)
Error budget — 1 − SLO: how much downtime/error is acceptable in a period (99.9% → 43 min/month)
Error budget burn rate — rate at which budget is consumed; fast burn = imminent SLO violation
MTTR — Mean Time to Recovery: key reliability metric; minimize with runbooks + automation
MTBF — Mean Time Between Failures; maximize with fault isolation and redundancy
RTO — Recovery Time Objective: max acceptable downtime (DR planning)
RPO — Recovery Point Objective: max acceptable data loss (backup frequency)
Multi-AZ deployment — replicate across availability zones for HA within a region
Multi-region deployment — replicate across regions for DR; active-active vs active-passive
Active-active failover — both regions serve traffic; complex consistency, zero downtime
Active-passive failover — primary serves all traffic; secondary on standby; DNS failover
Chaos engineering — intentionally inject failures: kill random pods (Chaos Monkey), Gremlin
Game days — scheduled chaos: simulate region outage, practice incident response with real team
Graceful degradation — serve reduced functionality when dependency fails (disable recommendations, show cached data)
Bulkhead isolation — separate thread pools and connection pools per downstream dependency
Three pillars of observability — logs (what happened), metrics (how much), traces (how long and where)
Four golden signals (Google SRE) — latency, traffic (RPS), errors (rate), saturation (utilization)
RED method — Rate (requests/sec), Errors (rate), Duration (latency distribution)
USE method — Utilization, Saturation, Errors per resource (CPU, memory, disk, network)
Structured logging — JSON format: include trace_id, span_id, request_id, user_id, service_name
Log levels — TRACE (verbose), DEBUG, INFO (business events), WARN (recoverable), ERROR (needs action), FATAL
Log aggregation — Fluentd/Logstash collect → Elasticsearch store → Kibana visualize (ELK/EFK)
Prometheus data model — time series labeled by key-value pairs; pull-based scraping
Prometheus metric types — Counter (monotone: total_requests), Gauge (current: active_connections), Histogram (latency buckets), Summary
PromQL queries — rate(http_requests_total[5m]), histogram_quantile(0.99, ...), topk(5, ...)
Grafana — connect to Prometheus/CloudWatch/InfluxDB; build dashboards, set alert thresholds
Distributed tracing — trace = end-to-end request; span = single operation with start/end/metadata
OpenTelemetry — vendor-neutral SDK for traces, metrics, logs; single integration for all backends
W3C TraceContext — traceparent and tracestate headers for cross-service trace propagation
Jaeger / Zipkin — open-source distributed tracing backends; Tempo (Grafana), X-Ray (AWS)
APM tools — Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace: trace + metrics + logs in one platform
Alerting best practices — alert on SLO burn rate, not raw metrics; PagerDuty + runbooks for every alert
P50/P99/P99.9 latency — mean misleads; tail latency (P99.9) matters at scale (1 in 1000 requests)
Tail latency mitigation — hedged requests: send duplicate to second server if first exceeds threshold, use first response
On-call best practices — runbooks, escalation policy, post-mortems, blameless culture, rotation fairness
Profiling — CPU flame graphs (async-profiler, py-spy), heap dumps, I/O tracing (strace, perf)
Flame graph — visualize hot code paths; identify unexpected CPU consumers in production
Load testing — k6, Locust, Apache JMeter, wrk; always test in staging environment first
Stress testing — find breaking point (max RPS before error rate spikes)
Soak testing — sustained load for hours; catch memory leaks, connection pool exhaustion
Spike testing — sudden 10× traffic increase; test auto-scaling and DB connection pool behavior
Little's Law in practice — L = λW: if p99 latency increases, L (queue depth) grows; fix by reducing W or λ
Connection pool sizing — formula: pool = (cores × 2) + effective_spindle_count; too large → context switch overhead
Thread pool sizing — I/O-bound: threads = (1 + wait_time/service_time) × cores; CPU-bound: threads ≈ cores
Async I/O and non-blocking — event loop (Node.js, Netty, asyncio): single thread handles thousands of I/O connections
N+1 query — detect via slow query log or ORM verbose mode; fix with JOIN, eager loading, or DataLoader
Batch APIs — reduce round trips: fetch 100 items in one request vs 100 individual requests (10× improvement)
Compression — Snappy (fastest, moderate ratio), LZ4 (balanced), gzip (best ratio, slower), Zstandard (best of both)
Efficient serialization — Protocol Buffers 3–10× smaller than JSON; Avro for Kafka schemas; MessagePack for binary JSON
GC tuning (JVM) — G1GC for balanced latency; ZGC for sub-ms GC pauses; tune heap: not too small (frequent GC), not too large (long GC)
Database connection exhaustion — symptom: timeout waiting for connection; fix: pool size + circuit breaker upstream
Right-sizing compute — use CloudWatch metrics to identify over-provisioned instances
Spot / preemptible instances — 70–90% savings; design stateless workers that handle 2-min shutdown notice
Reserved instances vs savings plans — 1–3 year commitment for 30–60% discount on baseline capacity
S3 storage tiering — Standard → Standard-IA → Glacier Instant → Glacier Flexible → Deep Archive
Lifecycle policies — auto-transition objects to cheaper tier after 30/90/365 days
Data transfer costs — same-AZ is free; cross-AZ costs $0.01/GB; cross-region higher; CDN reduces egress
Caching ROI — every cache hit saves a DB query; measure cache hit rate, aim for >95% for hot paths
Compression reduces bandwidth and storage — 3–10× reduction for JSON/text data
Auto-scaling to zero — Lambda, Cloud Run, ECS Fargate: no cost when no traffic (ideal for batch workloads)
Database read replicas cost tradeoff — cheaper than sharding; only add when primary is read-saturated

note: Know the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation). For every service you design, specify: what SLO would you set? What would you alert on? How would you debug a latency spike at 3am? This shows production engineering maturity.

title: Fintech & Banking Systems
pri: Visa, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, Goldman: expect payment/ledger/trading flavoured designs
note: Money rules: integers in paise, idempotency at every hop, timeout ≠ failure, double-entry append-only ledger, outbox for events, daily reconciliation, tokenize card data.

tops: Card payment parties — cardholder, merchant, acquirer/PSP, card network, issuer
Authorization vs capture vs settlement — hold now, claim later, move money in batch
UPI flow — payer PSP → NPCI → remitter bank → beneficiary bank
Payment state machine — CREATED → PROCESSING → AUTHORIZED/FAILED/UNKNOWN → CAPTURED → SETTLED/REFUNDED
Refunds, reversals & chargebacks — undoing money movement safely
PSP webhooks & status polling — resolving UNKNOWN payments
Representing money — integer minor units or BigDecimal, never float
Idempotency at every hop — client→API, API→PSP, consumers, webhooks
Double-entry ledger — every transaction has balanced debits and credits
Ledger immutability — append-only entries, fix with reversing entries
Reconciliation — match internal records with bank/PSP settlement files
Exactly-once money movement — at-least-once + idempotency + state guards + reconciliation
Hot accounts — sub-accounts and batching for high-write ledger accounts
PCI-DSS & tokenization — keep card numbers out of most systems
Fraud & risk checks — rules, velocity limits, ML scoring in the payment path
RBI data localisation & audit trails — data stays in India, immutable logs
Order book & matching engine — price-time priority, single-threaded per symbol
Low-latency techniques — LMAX Disruptor, GC avoidance, kernel bypass
Market data fan-out — multicast, conflation, sequence numbers

title: Low-Level Design (OOD) in Java
pri: Machine-coding / LLD rounds at banks and Bangalore product companies
note: Clarify → entities → class diagram → interfaces → code the core flow → extend with patterns → concurrency & edge cases. Keep it runnable.

tops: Four pillars — encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism
SOLID principles — SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP
Composition over inheritance — has-a beats deep hierarchies
Creational — Singleton, Factory, Builder
Strategy pattern — swap algorithms at runtime
Observer pattern — notify subscribers of changes
State pattern — behaviour changes with lifecycle state
Decorator & Adapter — wrap to add behaviour or translate interfaces
Chain of Responsibility — pass requests along handlers
Machine-coding approach — requirements, entities, classes, code, tests in 90 minutes
Java concurrency toolkit — locks, atomics, ConcurrentHashMap, executors
Thread-safe singleton — holder idiom, enum, double-checked locking
Per-resource locking — CAS on the resource instead of one global lock
